title: Gaudete
hook: the third Sunday of Advent is rose-colored: rejoice, the Lord is near

segments.voice: Yesterday, Advent's second Sunday: John in the wilderness, clearing the road. Your line was prepare the way.

Rose. Not purple. Partway through a season of waiting, of violet cloth and serious readings, the priest in some churches walks out on the third Sunday wearing pink. On the wreath, the earlier candles have burned down a little, and now a rose-colored one is lit beside them. It looks almost like a mistake. It isn't. The Sunday has a name, and the name is a single Latin word, an order and an invitation at once.

Gaudete means rejoice. It's the first word of the old Latin chant sung as the Mass begins on this Sunday, and the chant comes from Paul's letter to the Philippians. In the King James Bible: "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice." A line later, the reason: "The Lord is at hand." Near. Close enough to touch. Here's what makes it hard to dismiss as cheerful talk. Paul writes this letter in chains. Earlier in it he mentions "my bonds in Christ", and he isn't sure whether he'll live or die. A prisoner, telling free people to rejoice, twice. So Gaudete Sunday isn't a party thrown because the waiting is over. It's a lighter color in the middle of the waiting, because what's coming is nearer than it was. Tradition says the rose is purple brightened, joy breaking into the fast. Churches keep the day differently. Catholics, and some Anglicans and Lutherans, may wear rose vestments and keep the Latin name. Other churches simply light a pink candle, sometimes calling it the candle of joy. Others keep blue or purple all the way through. And right after the line about the Lord being near, Paul goes on: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God." Careful there means anxious. Don't be eaten up by worry; bring it to God, with thanks. That's Gaudete's kind of joy: not pretending the chains aren't there, but rejoicing because someone is near.

segments.voice: Let one good thing come to mind, small and specific: the way the light hit the kitchen this morning, a message from a friend, a meal. Let the worries wait outside for a moment, and just be glad of it. If you pray, you can give thanks with Paul's line, rejoice in the Lord alway; if you don't, simply stay with the gladness.
Gaudete. Latin for rejoice: the name of Advent's third Sunday, rose-colored, from Paul's words, rejoice in the Lord alway, the Lord is at hand.
Your line: rejoice, he is near. Joy can break into the waiting. Rose Sunday, done.

howItsDone: On the third Sunday of Advent, Catholic and some Anglican and Lutheran churches use rose-colored vestments and light a rose candle on the Advent wreath, often hearing Philippians 4:4–7; other churches light a pink candle of joy.

notes: 'the first word of the old Latin chant sung as the Mass begins' (the Introit of the Third Sunday of Advent, 'Gaudete in Domino semper'): not stated in the cited biblical text; confirm.
'Tradition says the rose is purple brightened, joy breaking into the fast' is attributed; confirm. The parallel use of rose on Laetare Sunday in Lent is left out.
Church practice (Catholics and some Anglicans and Lutherans with rose vestments; others with a pink candle of joy; others blue or purple throughout) is general and unranked; confirm.
Hook says 'two purple candles are already burnt down a little': assumes a wreath with purple first and second candles; some use blue. Confirm or soften.
'Careful there means anxious' glosses the KJV's older sense of 'careful'; confirm.
Philippians 1:20–24 is paraphrased as 'he isn't sure whether he'll live or die'.
